items.readable_text:
Content:
The additive inverse of [MATH: a] modulo [MATH: n] is the integer [MATH: 0 \leq x \lt n] such that

Content:
[MATH: x + a \equiv 0 \quad (\textrm{mod} \: n).]

Content:
For example, the integer [MATH: 7] is the additive inverse of [MATH: 5] modulo [MATH: 12] since
[MATH: 7 + 5≡12≡0(mod12).]

Content:
We can visualize this using a clock diagram.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/23cae19e874713ddc413f2f777a4997c]

Content:
On the other hand, the integer [MATH: 6] is not the additive inverse of [MATH: 5] modulo [MATH: 12] since [MATH: 6 + 5 \equiv 11\not\equiv 0 \, (\textrm{mod} \: 12).]

Content:
In general, we have the following theorem:

Content:
> For every integer, there exists a unique additive inverse for a given modulus [MATH: n.]

Content:
Note the following:

Content:
- The word "unique" in the statement above means with respect to the inequality [MATH: 0 \leq x \lt n.]
- It's important to know that any integer summed with an integer congruent to its inverse will also give zero.

For example, [MATH: x=7] is the additive inverse of [MATH: 5] modulo [MATH: 12.] But since [MATH: 19\equiv 7\:(\textrm{mod}\: 12),] we have that the sum of [MATH: 5] and [MATH: 19] is also congruent to [MATH: 0{:}]
[MATH: 19 + 5≡24≡2 ⋅ 12≡0(mod12)]

Content:
Let's see some more examples.

sections.normalized_html:
Is the following statement true or false?

The integer [MATH: 21] is the additive inverse of [MATH: 14] modulo [MATH: 35.]
sections.readable_text:
Is the following statement true or false?

> The integer [MATH: 21] is the additive inverse of [MATH: 14] modulo [MATH: 35.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The additive inverse of [MATH: 14] modulo [MATH: 35] is the integer [MATH: 0 \leq x \lt 35] such that

[MATH: x + 14 \equiv 0 \quad (\textrm{mod}\:35).]

Now, notice that when we add our two numbers, we get a number that is congruent to zero modulo [MATH: 35{:}]

[MATH: 21 + 14|≡35|(mod35); ≡0|(mod35)]

Therefore, the statement is true.

sections.normalized_html: Find the additive inverse of [MATH: 17] modulo [MATH: 26.]
sections.readable_text: Find the additive inverse of [MATH: 17] modulo [MATH: 26.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The additive inverse of [MATH: 17] modulo [MATH: 26] is the integer [MATH: 0 \leq x \lt 26] such that

[MATH: x + 17 \equiv 0 \quad (\textrm{mod}\:26).]

Notice that [MATH: -17 + 17 \equiv 0,] so [MATH: x\equiv -17\:(\textrm{mod}\:26).] To write this in the required form, we use the following sequence of congruences:

[MATH: x|≡ − 17|(mod26); ≡0 − 17|(mod26); ≡26 − 17|(mod26); ≡9|(mod26)]

Therefore, the additive inverse of the element [MATH: 17] modulo [MATH: 26] is [MATH: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}9}.]

We can verify this result as follows: [MATH: 9 + 17 \equiv 26 \equiv 0\:\:{\color{green}{\checkmark}} \quad (\textrm{mod}\:26)]

Note: The additive inverse of [MATH: a] modulo [MATH: n] is simply the residue of [MATH: -a] modulo [MATH: n,] i.e. [MATH: -a \: \textrm{mod} \: n.]

sections.normalized_html: Find the additive inverse of [MATH: 23] modulo [MATH: 15.]
sections.readable_text: Find the additive inverse of [MATH: 23] modulo [MATH: 15.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The additive inverse of [MATH: 23] modulo [MATH: 15] is the integer [MATH: 0 \leq x \lt 15] such that

[MATH: x + 23 \equiv 0 \quad (\textrm{mod}\:15).]

First, we note that [MATH: 23\equiv 8\:(\textrm{mod}\:15){:}] [MATH: 23|≡1 ⋅ 15 + 8|(mod15); ≡1 ⋅ 0 + 8|(mod15); ≡8|(mod15)]

Also, note that [MATH: -8 + 8 \equiv 0,] so [MATH: x\equiv -8\:(\textrm{mod}\:15).] To write this in the required form, we use the following sequence of congruences:

[MATH: x|≡ − 8|(mod15); ≡0 − 8|(mod15); ≡15 − 8|(mod15); ≡7|(mod15)]

Therefore, the additive inverse of the element [MATH: 23] modulo [MATH: 15] is [MATH: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}7}.]

We can verify this result as follows: [MATH: 23 + 7≡30≡2 ⋅ 15≡0✓(mod15)]

Note: In general, the additive inverse of [MATH: a] modulo [MATH: n] is simply the residue of [MATH: -a] modulo [MATH: n,] i.e. [MATH: -a \: \textrm{mod} \: n.]

sections.normalized_html: Find the additive inverse of [MATH: -43] modulo [MATH: 15.]
sections.readable_text: Find the additive inverse of [MATH: -43] modulo [MATH: 15.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The additive inverse of [MATH: -43] modulo [MATH: 15] is the integer [MATH: 0 \leq x \lt 15] such that

[MATH: x + (-43) \equiv 0 \quad (\textrm{mod}\:15).]

First, we note that [MATH: -43\equiv 2\:(\textrm{mod}\:15){:}] [MATH: − 43|≡(− 3) ⋅ 15 + 2|(mod15); ≡(− 3) ⋅ 0 + 2|(mod15); ≡2|(mod15)]

Also, note that [MATH: -2 + 2 \equiv 0,] so [MATH: x\equiv -2\:(\textrm{mod}\:15).] To write this in the required form, we use the following sequence of congruences:

[MATH: x|≡ − 2|(mod15); ≡0 − 2|(mod15); ≡15 − 2|(mod15); ≡13|(mod15)]

Therefore, the additive inverse of the element [MATH: -43] modulo [MATH: 15] is [MATH: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}13}.]

We can verify this result as follows: [MATH: − 43 + 13≡ − 30≡(− 2) ⋅ 15≡0✓(mod15)]

Note: In general, the additive inverse of [MATH: a] modulo [MATH: n] is simply the residue of [MATH: -a] modulo [MATH: n,] i.e. [MATH: -a \: \textrm{mod} \: n.]
